title: Parallel Systems — GPU Orchestration and Optimization for AI Workloads
content:
Parallel Systems is the GPU orchestration platform that makes AI infrastructure work harder. We help enterprises maximize the performance of every GPU in their fleet — cutting compute costs by over 60% while improving workload throughput.

Most enterprises use only 30-40% of their GPU capacity. The rest is wasted — idle cycles, inefficient scheduling, poor workload distribution across heterogeneous hardware. At current GPU prices, that waste translates to millions of dollars per year for any serious AI operation.

Parallel Systems fixes this. Our orchestration engine dynamically schedules AI workloads across GPU clusters — including mixed hardware environments with H100s, A100s, and older generation cards — maximizing utilization to 80% or higher. We work across multi-cloud and on-premise environments, giving enterprises a single control plane for their entire AI compute infrastructure.

Founded in 2023 by Ryan Tanaka, former Google Brain infrastructure lead, and Dr. Maria Santos, formerly of Meta FAIR with a PhD in distributed systems from MIT, Parallel Systems is built by the team that understands GPU infrastructure at the deepest level. Ryan built the system that trains Google's largest models. Maria designed distributed training architectures used by some of the world's largest AI labs.

Our 40-person team in San Francisco serves 28 enterprise customers, from AI-native startups to Fortune 500 companies, managing billions of GPU-hours annually. Backed by Greylock.

The reasons: poor scheduling (workloads sit idle waiting for specific GPU types), lack of multi-cluster coordination, inability to use heterogeneous hardware efficiently. At $2-3/hour per H100, this waste is enormous.

- **Solution**: Parallel Systems provides an orchestration layer that sits above GPU clusters (cloud, on-prem, or hybrid) and dynamically schedules workloads for maximum utilization. Their engine understands workload characteristics (training vs inference, batch size, memory requirements) and GPU capabilities (H100 vs A100 vs V100) and optimally assigns work. Result: utilization goes from 30-40% to 80%+.

- **Traction**: 28 enterprise customers. $3.2M ARR. Growing 35% QoQ. Customer base includes major AI labs, tech companies, and traditional enterprises running AI workloads. Average deal size $115K/year.

- **Fundraise**: Series A, targeting ~$20M. $8M seed from Greylock (2023). Targeting $70M pre-money valuation.

## My Assessment

This could be huge. GPU costs are the universal pain point in AI right now. Every portfolio company complains about it. Every enterprise AI team I talk to lists it as their top infrastructure challenge. If Parallel Systems becomes the default orchestration layer, this is a foundational infrastructure company.

title: Parallel Systems — Technical Deep-Dive with Dr. Maria Santos (CTO)
author: Maya Patel
content:
Meeting: Technical deep-dive — Parallel Systems
Date: February 12, 2026
Attendees: Maya Patel (AIVC), Dr. Maria Santos (CTO, Parallel Systems)
Location: Parallel Systems office, San Francisco (+ screen share demo)

## Summary

2.5-hour deep session with Maria. This is the most technically sophisticated infrastructure product I've evaluated in the past year. Maria is exceptional — rare combination of deep systems knowledge and practical product thinking.

## Technical Architecture

- **Orchestration Engine**: The core system operates as a real-time workload scheduler. It maintains a continuously updated model of cluster state (GPU availability, memory, current utilization, thermal status, network topology) and workload requirements (compute, memory, communication patterns, deadline constraints). Scheduling decisions are made using a combination of constraint optimization and ML-based prediction.

- **Heterogeneous GPU Support**: This is a key differentiator. Most orchestration tools assume homogeneous clusters (all H100s or all A100s). Parallel Systems works across mixed hardware — H100, A100, V100, even older T4s. The engine understands the performance characteristics of each GPU type and assigns workloads accordingly. Training jobs that need H100 interconnect get H100s. Inference workloads that don't need the latest hardware get routed to A100s or V100s.

- **Multi-Cloud**: Works across AWS, GCP, Azure, and on-premise. Single control plane. This is where many competitors fall short — they're optimized for one cloud provider. Parallel Systems' abstraction layer lets enterprises use the cheapest available GPUs across providers.

- **Benchmarks**: Maria showed real customer data. Average utilization improvement: 30-40% baseline to 80-85% with Parallel Systems. Translates to 2.3x cost reduction on average. One customer (AI startup running large training jobs) went from $800K/month GPU spend to $340K/month.

## Competitive Moat Assessment

- **Strengths**: Multi-cloud heterogeneous GPU orchestration is genuinely hard. The scheduling algorithms require deep understanding of GPU hardware, ML workload patterns, and distributed systems. Maria's academic background (her MIT PhD thesis was on dynamic scheduling in heterogeneous clusters) is directly relevant.

- **Major Concern — Nvidia**: Nvidia acquired Run:ai for $700M in February. Run:ai was building GPU orchestration (primarily for on-prem). If Nvidia builds native orchestration into its CUDA toolkit and DGX Cloud, it could become the default. Maria's counter: Nvidia will optimize for Nvidia hardware only. Parallel Systems' multi-cloud, multi-hardware approach is fundamentally different. Enterprise customers don't want to be locked into one GPU vendor.

## Technical Assessment

- **Innovation**: 9/10 — The heterogeneous multi-cloud orchestration is genuinely best-in-class. I haven't seen another company handle this with this level of sophistication.

- **Engineering Quality**: 9/10 — Clean architecture, real benchmarks, production-hardened. Maria's team is world-class.

- **Defensibility**: 7/10 — High because of technical complexity, but Nvidia looms large. The multi-vendor angle is the key differentiator.

- [ ] Request access to technical documentation and architecture diagrams
- [ ] Discuss Nvidia competitive risk with Sarah in detail

title: GPU Shortage Drives Enterprise Demand for AI Infrastructure Optimization Tools
author: Sharon Goldman
content:
GPU Shortage Drives Enterprise Demand for AI Infrastructure Optimization Tools
By Sharon Goldman | VentureBeat | January 28, 2026

As the GPU shortage enters its third year, enterprises are increasingly turning to software tools that help them squeeze more out of the GPUs they already have.

A new crop of startups — including Parallel Systems, Anyscale, and CoreWeave — is capitalizing on the reality that most enterprises use only a fraction of their GPU capacity. According to a recent survey by Gartner, the average enterprise achieves just 35% utilization of its GPU fleet, meaning billions of dollars of compute capacity sits idle.

"The GPU shortage isn't just about supply," said Ryan Tanaka, CEO of Parallel Systems, whose software helps enterprises orchestrate AI workloads across GPU clusters. "It's about utilization. Most companies have enough GPUs — they just use them badly."

Parallel Systems, founded in 2023 by former Google Brain infrastructure lead Tanaka and ex-Meta FAIR researcher Dr. Maria Santos, claims its orchestration platform can improve GPU utilization to 80% or more. The San Francisco-based company has raised $8 million in seed funding from Greylock Partners and says it serves 28 enterprise customers.

The GPU optimization market is attracting attention from the biggest player in the space: Nvidia itself. The chipmaker is understood to be exploring infrastructure software that could complement its hardware dominance, though details remain scarce.

Anyscale, the company behind the popular open-source Ray framework, has also been expanding its enterprise offering, while CoreWeave continues to build out its GPU cloud infrastructure. Each represents a different approach to the same fundamental problem: making AI compute more accessible and affordable.

"We estimate the GPU optimization and orchestration market will reach $8 billion by 2028," said Forrester analyst David Kim. "Every enterprise running AI workloads at scale needs better GPU management tools."

title: Parallel Systems Helps Enterprises Cut GPU Costs by 60%, Backed by Greylock
author: Kenrick Cai
content:
Parallel Systems Helps Enterprises Cut GPU Costs by 60%, Backed by Greylock
By Kenrick Cai | Forbes AI | March 10, 2026

Ryan Tanaka spent five years at Google building the infrastructure that trains the company's most powerful AI models. He saw firsthand how even the most sophisticated AI operation in the world struggled with GPU efficiency.

"At Google, we had some of the best infrastructure engineers on the planet, and we still had utilization problems," Tanaka told Forbes from his San Francisco office. "If Google struggles with this, imagine what every other company goes through."

That insight led Tanaka to co-found Parallel Systems in 2023 with Dr. Maria Santos, a former Meta AI researcher and MIT-trained distributed systems expert. The company has built a GPU orchestration platform that, according to its customers, reduces compute costs by more than 60% by dramatically improving how enterprises use their GPU resources.

The problem Parallel Systems addresses is deceptively simple: most enterprises use only 30-40% of their GPU capacity. Workloads are scheduled inefficiently, different GPU models are poorly matched to different tasks, and multi-cloud environments create coordination chaos. Parallel Systems' software sits on top of GPU infrastructure and optimizes all of it automatically.

The results, according to Tanaka, are dramatic. "Our average customer sees 2.3x cost reduction within the first month. One customer went from spending $800,000 a month on GPU compute to $340,000 — same workloads, same results, just better orchestration."

Parallel Systems has attracted 28 enterprise customers and recently crossed $3 million in annual recurring revenue, growing approximately 35% quarter over quarter. The company raised an $8 million seed round from Greylock Partners in 2023 and is understood to be in discussions for a Series A round.

The competitive landscape is evolving rapidly. Nvidia's $700 million acquisition of GPU orchestration startup Run:ai in February sent a clear signal that the chip giant sees infrastructure software as strategic. But Tanaka argues Parallel Systems' multi-vendor approach is actually strengthened by Nvidia's move.

"Nvidia building native orchestration for Nvidia hardware is actually good for us," Tanaka said. "It validates the category and it makes enterprises more aware that they need this kind of tool. But enterprises don't want to be locked into one vendor's ecosystem. We're the Switzerland of GPU orchestration — we work with everyone."

title: Nvidia Acquires Run:ai for $700M to Build GPU Orchestration Into Its Stack
author: Stephen Nellis
content:
Nvidia Acquires Run:ai for $700M to Build GPU Orchestration Into Its Stack
By Stephen Nellis | Reuters | February 5, 2026

SANTA CLARA — Nvidia said on Wednesday it had acquired Run:ai, an Israeli startup specializing in GPU orchestration software, for approximately $700 million in cash, as the chipmaker deepens its push into infrastructure software.

The acquisition gives Nvidia a software platform that helps enterprises manage and optimize workloads across GPU clusters — a capability Nvidia plans to integrate into its DGX Cloud offering and CUDA ecosystem.

"AI infrastructure is not just about hardware. It's about the software that makes that hardware work at its full potential," said Jensen Huang, Nvidia's CEO. "Run:ai gives us the orchestration layer that completes our full-stack AI infrastructure vision."

Run:ai, founded in 2018 in Tel Aviv, had raised approximately $118 million in venture funding. Its software helps organizations pool and dynamically allocate GPU resources across teams and workloads, improving utilization rates. The company worked primarily with on-premise GPU deployments.

The deal validates the growing market for GPU orchestration tools but raises competitive questions for startups in the space. Companies like Parallel Systems, which offers similar orchestration capabilities for multi-cloud and hybrid environments, could face pressure as Nvidia bundles orchestration into its hardware and cloud offerings.

"This is the natural evolution of Nvidia's strategy — owning the full stack from chips to software," said Stacy Rasgon, a semiconductor analyst at Bernstein. "The question for independent GPU orchestration companies is whether enterprises will pay for a third-party tool when Nvidia offers one natively."

However, some enterprise customers and analysts noted that Nvidia's approach may reinforce vendor lock-in concerns. "We use GPUs from multiple vendors and run across multiple clouds," said one CTO at a major AI company who declined to be named. "A Nvidia-native orchestration tool doesn't solve our problem. We need something that works across our entire infrastructure."

Run:ai's team will join Nvidia's enterprise software division in Santa Clara. The acquisition is expected to close in Q2 2026, subject to regulatory approval.

title: Anyscale Raises $100M Series C for Ray-Based AI Infrastructure
author: Kyle Wiggers
content:
Anyscale Raises $100M Series C for Ray-Based AI Infrastructure
By Kyle Wiggers | TechCrunch | March 18, 2026

Anyscale, the company behind the popular open-source distributed computing framework Ray, has raised $100 million in Series C funding led by Addition with participation from existing investors including a16z and Intel Capital. The round values the company at $1.2 billion.

Anyscale's platform enables enterprises to scale AI workloads — from data processing to model training to inference — across clusters of GPUs and CPUs. Built on the Ray framework, which was developed at UC Berkeley's RISELab and is now used by companies including Uber, Spotify, and OpenAI, the platform provides a unified runtime for distributed AI applications.

"Ray is becoming the default execution layer for AI workloads," said Anyscale CEO Robert Nishihara, who co-created Ray during his PhD at Berkeley. "With this funding, we're making it even easier for enterprises to run any AI workload at any scale."

The fundraise comes as the AI infrastructure market attracts significant capital and consolidation. Nvidia recently acquired GPU orchestration startup Run:ai for $700 million, while companies like Parallel Systems and Modal are also building GPU management and orchestration tools.

Anyscale's approach differs from pure orchestration companies like Parallel Systems in a key way: Ray is a general-purpose distributed computing framework, not specifically a GPU scheduler. While Parallel Systems focuses narrowly on GPU utilization optimization, Anyscale's platform handles the broader challenge of distributing any compute workload across any infrastructure.

"We're complementary to GPU orchestration tools in some cases," Nishihara acknowledged. "But as Ray's GPU scheduling capabilities improve, there's natural overlap."

Anyscale says it now has over 500 enterprise customers and is growing revenue at more than 100% year-over-year. The company plans to use the new funding to expand its enterprise sales team and invest in Ray's GPU scheduling and inference serving capabilities.
